summary:
Outpost Commander is an interactive, browser-based simulation and mission training game designed specifically for children ages 7–12 to explore space exploration and resource management. Developed as a web application using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, the project addresses the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by teaching young players real aerospace engineering trade-offs.

Players must balance critical habitat resources—Power, Life Support, and Radiation Shielding—while navigating dynamic environmental hazards like solar flares and multi-sol lunar night cycles. This project is important because it makes complex space science concepts engaging, accessible, and intuitive for kids, inspiring the next generation of space explorers through interactive play and zero-install browser accessibility.
details:
• What does it do and how does it work?
    Outpost Commander is a web-based simulation game where players manage a lunar or Martian habitat. Players make strategic resource management decisions across turns (Sols), balancing Power generation, Life Support stability, and Electromagnetic Shield integrity against environmental challenges like solar flares and dark lunar phases.
  • What benefits does it have & what is the intended impact?
    The game educates children ages 7–12 on aerospace engineering trade-offs, systems thinking, and space science. Its intended impact is to spark early curiosity in STEM fields and space exploration through gamified learning.
  • What tools, languages, and software did you use?
    The project was built using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+) for frontend game logic and dynamic SVG UI rendering, Web Audio API for interactive synthesized sound effects, and hosted via GitHub Pages.
  • How is your project creative?
    Unlike static quizzes or passive videos, Outpost Commander combines live animated habitat visuals, real NASA scientific grounding (such as ECLSS life support and solar weather constraints), and an interactive day/night hazard cycle that forces kids to plan ahead.
  • What factors did your team consider?
    We focused heavily on user experience (UX) for young children—ensuring high-contrast visual cues, intuitive touch/click controls, zero required downloads, and bite-sized educational pop-ups explaining real NASA missions.
